note.explanation: Atomic structure explains how protons, neutrons and electrons are arranged, why elements differ, and how isotopes and radioactivity behave.
examples: A neutral oxygen-16 atom has 8 protons, 8 electrons and 8 neutrons.
A neutral bismuth-210 atom has 210 − 83 = 127 neutrons.
note.checkAnswer: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons; its neutron number is mass number minus atomic number.
note.simple: An atom has a tiny nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons arranged around it. The number of protons identifies the element.
note.checkQuestion: How many neutrons are present in ²¹⁰₈₃Bi?
note.title: Atomic structure, isotopes and radioactivity
steps: Read the atomic number: it gives the number of protons.
For a neutral atom, set the number of electrons equal to the number of protons.
Subtract the atomic number from the mass number to find neutrons.
For relative atomic mass, multiply each isotope mass by its abundance and find the weighted mean.

mcqs.stem: Q2.1. How many electrons can be accommodated at the most in the third shell of the elements?
rationales: 8 is not the maximum capacity of the third shell.
18 is the maximum number of electrons in the third shell.
10 is fewer than the maximum capacity of the third shell.
32 is the maximum capacity of the fourth shell, not the third shell.

options: Structure of atom was discovered.
Neutrons and protons were discovered.
Electrons and protons were discovered.
Presence of nucleus in an atom was discovered.
mcqs.stem: Q2.2. What information was obtained from discharge tube experiments?
rationales: Discharge tube experiments revealed charged particles, not the complete structure of the atom.
The discharge tube experiments did not discover neutrons and protons together.
Discharge tube experiments led to the discovery of electrons and positive particles (protons).
The nucleus was identified through scattering experiments, not discharge tube experiments.

options: Periodic table cannot accommodate a large number of isotopes of different elements.
Some of the isotopes are unstable and they give rise to different elements
All the isotopes have same atomic number; so there is no need to give them separate places.
Isotopes do not show periodic behavior.
mcqs.stem: Q2.3. Why have isotopes not been shown in the periodic table?
rationales: The key reason is not a lack of space in the periodic table.
Instability of some isotopes does not explain why isotopes do not have separate places.
Isotopes have the same atomic number, so they occupy the same place in the periodic table.
Isotopes show the chemical behaviour associated with the same element and do not need separate places.

options: Electron
Neutron
Proton
Both neutron and electron
mcqs.stem: Q2.4. Which particle is present in different number in the isotopes?
rationales: Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons and, when neutral, electrons.
Isotopes of the same element differ in their number of neutrons.
The proton number is the same in all isotopes of an element.
Electrons do not differ between neutral isotopes of the same element; only the neutron number differs.

options: ¹⁷O
¹⁶O
¹⁸O
Non of these
mcqs.stem: Q2.5. In which isotope of oxygen there are the equal number of protons, electrons and neutrons?
rationales: Oxygen-17 has 8 protons, 8 electrons and 9 neutrons.
Oxygen-16 has 8 protons, 8 electrons and 8 neutrons.
Oxygen-18 has 8 protons, 8 electrons and 10 neutrons.
Oxygen-16 is an isotope that has equal numbers of all three particles.

mcqs.stem: Q2.6. What will be the relative atomic mass of nitrogen given the abundances of its two isotopes, ¹⁴N and ¹⁵N are 99.64 and 0.35 respectively.
rationales: This value is not obtained by weighting the two isotope masses by their given abundances.
Using the textbook weighted calculation, (14 × 99.64 + 15 × 0.35) ÷ 100 = 14.0021.
This value is much too high for a mixture made almost entirely of nitrogen-14.
This value is not the weighted mean of the given isotope masses and abundances.

options: It helps determine the age of organic matter.
It helps determine the composition of matter.
It helps determine the usefulness of matter.
It helps determine whether the matter is radioactive or not.
mcqs.stem: Q2.7. How is radiocarbon dating useful for archeologists?
rationales: Radiocarbon dating estimates the age of once-living organic material.
Radiocarbon dating is used to estimate age, not determine the material's composition.
It does not determine how useful a sample is.
It is a dating method and does not simply test whether a material is radioactive.

options: Particles are held together by strong nuclear force.
Particles are held together by weak nuclear force.
Particles are held together by electrostatic force.
Particles are held together by dipolar force.
mcqs.stem: Q2.8. What does keep the particles present in the nucleus intact?
rationales: The strong nuclear force binds particles in the nucleus together.
The weak nuclear force is not the force that holds the nucleus together.
Electrostatic repulsion between protons acts against the binding of the nucleus.
Dipolar force is not the force that holds nuclear particles together.

options: By keeping themselves stationary
By revolving around the nucleus
Due to their wave-like nature
A magnetic field around the nucleus keeps them away
mcqs.stem: Q2.9. How do electrons keep themselves away from the oppositely charged nucleus?
rationales: Electrons are not stationary in the classical model described in this question.
In the classical model, electrons revolve around the nucleus.
This is not the explanation given by the classical model in the options.
A magnetic field around the nucleus is not the explanation.

mcqs.stem: Q2.10. Rubidium consists of two isotopes ⁸⁵Rb and ⁸⁷Rb. The percent abundance of the light isotope is 72.2% What is the percent abundance of the heavier isotope? Its atomic mass is 85.47
rationales: 15% does not make the two isotope abundances add to 100%.
The two abundances add to 100%, so the heavier isotope is 100% − 72.2% = 27.8%.
37% does not make the two isotope abundances add to 100%.
72% is approximately the abundance of the lighter isotope, not the heavier one.

written.text: Why is it said that almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus?
written.finalAnswer: Almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus because protons and neutrons are in the nucleus and electrons have very little mass.

rubric.why: The answer must identify the massive particles and their location.
rubric.description: State that protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.
rubric.how: Name both particles and say they are located in the nucleus.

rubric.why: This explains why the nucleus accounts for almost all the atom's mass.
rubric.description: Compare the very small mass of electrons with that of nucleons.
rubric.how: State that electrons have very little mass compared with protons and neutrons.

modelAnswer: Protons and neutrons are present in the nucleus and have almost all the mass of the atom.
Electrons have very little mass compared with protons and neutrons.
Therefore, almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus.

written.text: Why are elements different from one another?
written.finalAnswer: Elements are different from one another because they have different numbers of protons in their nuclei.

rubric.why: The number of protons identifies an element.
rubric.description: Give the feature that differs between elements.
rubric.how: State that different elements have different numbers of protons.

rubric.why: This connects proton number with the identity of an element.
rubric.description: Relate proton number to atomic number or the nucleus.
rubric.how: Explain that proton number is the atomic number and determines the element.

modelAnswer: Elements have different numbers of protons in their nuclei.
The number of protons is the atomic number and determines the identity of the element.

written.text: How many neutrons are present in ²¹⁰₈₃Bi?

rubric.why: The neutron number is found by subtracting atomic number from mass number.
rubric.description: Show the correct subtraction.
rubric.how: Write 210 − 83.

rubric.why: The final neutron number must be correct.
rubric.description: Give the number of neutrons.
rubric.how: State 127 neutrons.

modelAnswer: Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number
= 127 neutrons

written.text: Why is tritium (³₁H) a radioactive element?
written.finalAnswer: Tritium is radioactive because its nucleus is unstable.

rubric.why: Radioactivity is caused by an unstable nucleus.
rubric.description: Identify that the tritium nucleus is unstable.
rubric.how: State that tritium has an unstable nucleus.

rubric.why: The answer should connect instability to radioactive change.
rubric.description: State that the unstable nucleus emits radiation or undergoes decay.
rubric.how: Explain that its nucleus changes by emitting radiation.

modelAnswer: Tritium has one proton and two neutrons in its nucleus.
This nucleus is unstable and emits radiation as it changes.
Therefore, tritium is radioactive.

written.text: How can an atom absorb and evolve energy?
written.finalAnswer: An atom absorbs energy when an electron moves to a higher energy shell and evolves energy when the electron falls to a lower energy shell.

rubric.why: Absorption is explained by an electron gaining energy and moving outward.
rubric.description: Explain how an atom absorbs energy.
rubric.how: State that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher energy shell.

rubric.why: Energy is released when an electron returns to a lower energy state.
rubric.description: Explain how an atom evolves or releases energy.
rubric.how: State that an electron moving to a lower energy shell releases energy.

modelAnswer: An atom absorbs energy when an electron moves from a lower energy shell to a higher energy shell.
An atom evolves energy when an electron moves from a higher energy shell to a lower energy shell.

written.text: Why does the energy of electron increase as we move from first shell to second shell?
written.finalAnswer: The electron in the second shell is farther from the nucleus and has greater energy than an electron in the first shell.

rubric.why: The shell's distance from the nucleus is central to the explanation.
rubric.description: Compare the positions of the first and second shells.
rubric.how: State that the second shell is farther from the nucleus.

rubric.why: A more distant electron is attracted less strongly to the nucleus.
rubric.description: Explain the effect of greater distance on attraction.
rubric.how: State that the nuclear attraction on the farther electron is weaker.

rubric.why: The answer must link shell position to electron energy.
rubric.description: State that the second shell has greater energy.
rubric.how: Compare the energy of an electron in the second shell with one in the first.

rubric.why: A complete answer makes the distance-and-energy relationship clear.
rubric.description: Give the final reason in a clear comparison.
rubric.how: Conclude that an electron farther from the nucleus has greater energy.

modelAnswer: The second shell is farther from the nucleus than the first shell.
The electron in the second shell is attracted less strongly by the nucleus.
It has greater energy than an electron in the first shell.

written.text: Why is it needed to lower the pressure of the gas inside the discharge tube?
written.finalAnswer: The gas pressure is lowered so that gas particles do not collide frequently and the charged particles can move through the tube.

rubric.why: The answer must identify the condition used in the tube.
rubric.description: State that the gas is kept at low pressure.
rubric.how: Say that the pressure of gas inside the tube is lowered.

rubric.why: Low pressure reduces collisions between gas particles.
rubric.description: Explain the effect of lowering pressure on collisions.
rubric.how: State that gas particles collide less frequently.

rubric.why: The particles must be able to travel through the tube.
rubric.description: State that charged particles can move through the gas.
rubric.how: Mention that electrons or charged particles travel through the tube.

rubric.why: This connects the low-pressure condition to the experiment.
rubric.description: Relate the particle movement to the discharge tube experiment.
rubric.how: Explain that the reduced collisions allow the discharge or rays to pass through the tube.

modelAnswer: The gas pressure inside a discharge tube is lowered.
At low pressure, gas particles are farther apart and collide less frequently.
The charged particles can then move through the tube and produce the observed discharge.

written.text: What is the classical concept of an electron? How has this concept changed with time?
written.finalAnswer: The classical concept described an electron as a particle revolving around the nucleus in a definite path. Later, its wave-like nature was recognised, and its exact position and path cannot be specified in the same way.

rubric.why: The classical description treats the electron as a particle.
rubric.description: State the classical view of an electron.
rubric.how: Describe the electron as a particle.

rubric.why: The classical model describes electron motion around the nucleus.
rubric.description: Give the classical electron motion.
rubric.how: State that the electron revolves around the nucleus in a definite path.

rubric.why: The later view includes the wave-like nature of electrons.
rubric.description: State how the concept changed.
rubric.how: Mention that electrons also show wave-like behaviour.

rubric.why: The modern description does not assign an exact classical path.
rubric.description: Explain the consequence of the changed concept.
rubric.how: State that the exact position or definite path cannot be specified as in the classical model.

modelAnswer: In the classical concept, an electron is a particle revolving around the nucleus in a definite path.
With time, the wave-like nature of the electron was recognised.
Therefore, an electron is not described as moving in an exactly known classical path.

written.text: Why the nuclei of the radioactive elements are unstable?
written.finalAnswer: The nuclei of radioactive elements are unstable because their neutron-to-proton ratio is not balanced, so they emit radiation to become more stable.

rubric.why: The question asks for the condition of radioactive nuclei.
rubric.description: Identify the nuclei as unstable.
rubric.how: State that radioactive elements have unstable nuclei.

rubric.why: The balance between neutrons and protons affects nuclear stability.
rubric.description: Give a cause of nuclear instability.
rubric.how: Explain that the neutron-to-proton balance is unsuitable.

rubric.why: Unstable nuclei undergo radioactive change.
rubric.description: State what the unstable nucleus does.
rubric.how: Mention emission of radiation or radioactive decay.

rubric.why: This explains the result of radioactive decay.
rubric.description: Give the outcome of the nuclear change.
rubric.how: Conclude that the nucleus changes towards greater stability.

modelAnswer: Radioactive elements have unstable nuclei.
Their neutron-to-proton ratio is not balanced.
The nuclei emit radiation and change towards a more stable condition.

written.text: During discharge tube experiments, how did the scientists conclude that the same type of electrons and protons are present in all the elements?
written.finalAnswer: The properties of cathode rays and positive rays were the same regardless of the gas or electrode material used, so scientists concluded that electrons and protons are common to all elements.

rubric.why: Cathode rays provided evidence for electrons.
rubric.description: Connect cathode rays with electrons.
rubric.how: State that cathode rays consist of electrons.

rubric.why: Positive rays provided evidence for positive particles.
rubric.description: Connect positive rays with protons.
rubric.how: State that positive rays show the presence of protons.

rubric.why: The consistent result across materials supports the conclusion.
rubric.description: Describe the consistency of the experimental result.
rubric.how: State that the rays or their properties were observed with different gases or electrode materials.

rubric.why: The answer must state the conclusion drawn by scientists.
rubric.description: Give the conclusion about the particles.
rubric.how: Conclude that electrons and protons are present in all elements.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays were obtained using different gases and electrode materials, and their properties remained the same.
Cathode rays consist of electrons.
Positive rays also showed the presence of positive particles (protons).
Scientists therefore concluded that electrons and protons are common to all elements.

written.text: Explain the structure of a hydrogen atom.
written.finalAnswer: A hydrogen atom has a nucleus containing one proton and one electron around the nucleus; in ordinary hydrogen (protium), the nucleus has no neutron.

rubric.why: A structural description must identify the nucleus.
rubric.description: Identify the central nucleus.
rubric.how: State that a hydrogen atom has a nucleus.

rubric.why: The proton is the positive particle in the hydrogen nucleus.
rubric.description: Give the proton number.
rubric.how: State that the nucleus contains one proton.

rubric.why: A neutral hydrogen atom has one electron.
rubric.description: Give the electron number.
rubric.how: State that the atom has one electron.

rubric.why: The answer must show how the electron is arranged relative to the nucleus.
rubric.description: Describe the electron's position.
rubric.how: State that the electron is arranged around the nucleus in its shell.

rubric.why: This completes the structure of the most common hydrogen isotope.
rubric.description: State the neutron number for ordinary hydrogen.
rubric.how: Mention that ordinary hydrogen (protium) has no neutron.

modelAnswer: A hydrogen atom has a small nucleus.
The nucleus of ordinary hydrogen (protium) contains one proton and no neutron.
One electron is arranged around the nucleus.
The atom is neutral because it has one proton and one electron.

written.text: How does the theory of atomic structure explain the ionization of atoms by a radioactive isotope?
written.finalAnswer: Radiation from a radioactive isotope transfers energy to atoms and removes electrons from them. The atoms left with fewer electrons become positive ions, while the removed electrons are free electrons.

rubric.why: The explanation begins with radiation from the radioactive source.
rubric.description: Identify the radiation source.
rubric.how: State that the radioactive isotope emits radiation.

rubric.why: The radiation must interact with atoms.
rubric.description: Describe the interaction of radiation with atoms.
rubric.how: State that the radiation transfers energy to atoms.

rubric.why: Ionization occurs when electrons are removed from atoms.
rubric.description: Explain how the atom is ionized.
rubric.how: State that electrons are knocked out or removed.

rubric.why: An atom missing electrons becomes positively charged.
rubric.description: Identify the resulting atom or ion.
rubric.how: State that the remaining atom becomes a positive ion.

rubric.why: The removed electrons are also products of ionization.
rubric.description: Identify the removed particles.
rubric.how: State that the ejected electrons become free electrons.

modelAnswer: A radioactive isotope emits radiation.
The radiation transfers energy to atoms in its path.
This energy removes electrons from the atoms.
The atoms that lose electrons become positive ions.
The removed electrons become free electrons.

written.text: What is radioactivity? Explain any three applications of radioactive isotopes.
written.finalAnswer: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus. Radioactive isotopes are used in medicine, in radiocarbon dating of organic matter, and as tracers in industry or agriculture.

rubric.why: The definition must state that an unstable nucleus emits radiation.
rubric.description: Define radioactivity.
rubric.how: Describe the spontaneous emission of radiation by an unstable nucleus.

rubric.why: A valid medical use is one application.
rubric.description: Give a medical application.
rubric.how: For example, state that radiation from isotopes is used to treat cancer.

rubric.why: Dating organic remains is an important application.
rubric.description: Give an application in archaeology or dating.
rubric.how: Explain that carbon-14 is used to estimate the age of organic matter.

rubric.why: A distinct practical application is needed.
rubric.description: Give a further application.
rubric.how: Mention the use of isotopes as tracers or in industrial testing.

rubric.why: The question asks for three applications, not just a definition.
rubric.description: Ensure that three applications are explained.
rubric.how: Give three different applications with a brief use for each.

modelAnswer: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus.
In medicine, radiation from radioactive isotopes can be used to treat cancer.
Carbon-14 is used in radiocarbon dating to estimate the age of organic matter.
Radioactive isotopes can be used as tracers to follow the movement of substances in industry or agriculture.

written.text:
Find out the relative atomic mass of mercury from the following data.

| Isotope | Relative Abundance | Isotope | Relative Abundance |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| ¹⁹⁶Hg | 0.0146% | ¹⁹⁹Hg | 16.34% |
| ¹⁹⁸Hg | 10.02% | ²⁰⁰Hg | 23.13% |
| ²⁰¹Hg | 13.22% | ²⁰²Hg | 29.80% |
| ²⁰⁴Hg | 6.85% | | |

rubric.why: Relative atomic mass is a weighted mean of isotope masses.
rubric.description: Choose the weighted-mean method.
rubric.how: Multiply each isotope mass by its abundance and divide by the total abundance.

rubric.why: The abundance-weighted contributions must be added correctly.
rubric.description: Calculate the weighted sum.
rubric.how: Show the sum of isotope mass multiplied by its listed abundance.

rubric.why: The listed abundances do not total 100%, so their actual total is used to normalize the mean.
rubric.description: Use the total listed abundance.
rubric.how: Add the provided percentages to obtain 99.3746%.

rubric.why: The final weighted mean is the requested result.
rubric.description: Give the relative atomic mass.
rubric.how: State the value to two decimal places and note that relative atomic mass has no unit.

modelAnswer: Relative atomic mass = Σ(isotope mass × relative abundance) ÷ Σ(relative abundance)
Weighted sum = 19939.0016
Relative atomic mass = 19939.0016 ÷ 99.3746 = 200.65 (no unit)

written.text: How can scientists synthesize elements in the laboratory?
written.finalAnswer: Scientists can synthesize elements by bombarding the nuclei of atoms with high-energy particles; nuclear reactions change the nuclei and can produce new elements.

rubric.why: Synthesis involves changing atomic nuclei, not ordinary chemical bonding.
rubric.description: Identify the process as a nuclear process.
rubric.how: State that scientists cause nuclear reactions.

rubric.why: The target nuclei are struck by energetic particles.
rubric.description: Name the particles used to bombard a target.
rubric.how: Give an example such as neutrons or ions.

rubric.why: The target nucleus must be changed by the reaction.
rubric.description: Explain what the particles strike.
rubric.how: State that the particles are directed at the nucleus of a target atom.

rubric.why: A new element is formed when the nuclear composition changes appropriately.
rubric.description: State the result of synthesis.
rubric.how: Conclude that the reaction can produce a nucleus of a new element.

modelAnswer: Scientists bombard the nuclei of selected atoms with high-energy particles such as neutrons or ions.
The particles cause a nuclear reaction in the target.
The nucleus changes and may form a new element.

written.text: A system just like our solar system exists in an atom. Comment on this statement.
written.finalAnswer: The statement is a useful early comparison: the nucleus is like the Sun and electrons are like planets around it. However, an atom is not exactly like a solar system because electrons show wave-like behaviour and are not simply planets moving in fixed paths.

rubric.why: The comparison identifies the central part of the atom.
rubric.description: Give the solar-system comparison for the nucleus.
rubric.how: Compare the nucleus with the Sun.

rubric.why: The comparison also describes electrons around the nucleus.
rubric.description: Give the comparison for electrons.
rubric.how: Compare electrons with planets moving around the Sun.

rubric.why: The question asks the student to comment, so the limitation must be noted.
rubric.description: State that the analogy is not fully accurate.
rubric.how: Explain that electrons are not simply tiny planets.

rubric.why: A modern feature of atomic structure distinguishes it from the solar-system model.
rubric.description: Give a reason the analogy has limits.
rubric.how: Mention electron wave-like behaviour or that electrons are not in simple fixed planetary paths.

modelAnswer: In an early comparison, the nucleus is like the Sun and the electrons are like planets around it.
This comparison helps show that the nucleus is central and electrons are arranged around it.
However, an atom is not exactly like a solar system.
Electrons show wave-like behaviour and are not simply planets moving in fixed paths.

examTips: Short questions commonly ask for particle counts, isotope differences, or a reason for a feature of atomic structure. State the key fact directly.
For a neutron-count question, write the formula first: number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number; then substitute and give the answer.
Constructed-response questions usually require a reason or a short explanation. Give the cause and then its consequence, rather than writing a single unsupported phrase.
For descriptive questions on applications, give the definition first and then explain three distinct applications with an example of what each is used for.
For relative atomic mass, show the weighted-mean formula, substitution for every isotope, the abundance total, and the final value. The working earns marks as well as the answer.
For investigative questions, make a clear comparison or conclusion and support it with at least one scientific reason.

explain.title: The atom and its nucleus
explain.body: An atom has a very small nucleus containing protons and neutrons. Electrons are arranged around the nucleus in shells. Almost all the atom's mass is in the nucleus because electrons have very little mass.

explain.title: Atomic number and neutron number
explain.body: The number of protons is the atomic number and identifies the element. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

explain.title: Electron shells and energy
explain.body: Electrons in shells farther from the nucleus have greater energy. An atom absorbs energy when an electron moves to a higher energy shell and evolves or releases energy when an electron moves to a lower energy shell.

explain.title: Isotopes and relative atomic mass
explain.body: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Their relative atomic mass is a weighted mean based on the abundance of each isotope.

explain.title: Radioactivity and its uses
explain.body: Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus. Radioactive isotopes have uses such as treating cancer, estimating the age of organic matter, and acting as tracers.

mistakes: Do not confuse mass number with atomic number: neutrons are found by subtracting atomic number from mass number.
Do not say isotopes have different numbers of protons. They have the same proton number and different neutron numbers.
Do not treat the electron as having a mass equal to a proton or neutron; its mass is very small.
When explaining energy absorption, say that the electron moves to a higher energy shell; emission occurs when it moves to a lower energy shell.
For weighted means, do not simply add isotope masses or ignore the abundances.
In descriptive answers, do not list applications of radioisotopes without saying what each application does.
For the mercury data printed here, the listed abundances add to 99.3746%, not 100%; show the total used in your calculation.
